claims.text: The studied material consists of sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles produced by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The as-deposited nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral morphologies.
The FCC structure of these nanoparticles is non-equilibrium and potentially maintained by kinetic trapping.
Atomic diffusion is sufficiently active in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles to permit substantial elemental redistribution despite the proposed sluggish-diffusion effect.
Surface segregation of Au and Cu is driven primarily by surface-energy minimization rather than sluggish bulk diffusion.
A critical temperature exists above which the surface-energy mechanism becomes dominant.
The mechanism becomes dominant when the surface-energy penalty of the initial non-equilibrium shape exceeds entropic stabilization energy.
Curvature-induced chemical-potential differences described by the Gibbs-Thomson effect drive elemental redistribution in these nanoparticles.
Au and Cu have sufficiently low surface energies relative to Co, Ni, and Pt that they preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-energy gradients allow redistribution through surface diffusion while bypassing the sluggish bulk-diffusion barrier.
The high surface-to-volume ratio supplies a thermodynamic driving force sufficient to overcome the kinetic barrier to atomic rearrangement.
Surface-energy reduction causes rapid surface diffusion and reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries.
Surface-enriched Au and Cu selectively evaporate before segregation or phase separation can proceed through bulk lattice diffusion.
Crossing the critical temperature will produce a sharp acceleration in particle loss and widening of the particle-size distribution.
Above the critical temperature, surviving particles will become spherical and will show Au/Cu-depleted cores together with transient Au/Cu surface enrichment.
The shape-evolution rate will correlate more strongly with initial aspect ratio than with bulk diffusion coefficients.
Sluggish diffusion can inhibit nanoscale growth or rearrangement in multicomponent alloys.
The proposed surface-energy mechanism applies only below 10 nm, fails above 50 nm, and requires an initially non-spherical particle.
